_about: Full-episode-only keys for scenarios/awareness_e16_insider_risk/scenario.json.erb (the E16 full shell). The wiring agent pastes each value into the full erb at the path its _notes line gives. None of these is carried into the generated defend-only shell by gen_e8_e17_shells.py EXCEPT concernForm: it is a DEFEND_HALF_KEY, so gen_e8_e17_shells.py defend_half_keys() copies it from this file into the defend-only shell too (E16 section 13); the sandbox and the montage stay full-only. Authored by opus48. ENG-04 (mistake stage + montage flip), ENG-12 (concernForm) and ENG-08 (schema) have landed. TONE (E16 section 18, a blocker): no blame, no surveillance framing; the flip ends on the kind, fair Samira outcome, and the concern form favours facts over a verdict.

beats.situation: Reuben is locked out with a report due at ten. "Can I just use yours? Two minutes."

options.label: Ring the service desk with him; they reset it in minutes

beats.situation: At lunch, Craig floats that Samira is leaving with Ross and taking the client list.

options.label: If he's actually seen something, point him to the security team or his manager, not the kitchen; otherwise leave it

beats.situation: An unknown contact messages you: "We pay people at firms like yours for remote access. 25% of what we make. Totally anonymous. Interested?"

options.label: Reply to find out how it works
Screenshot it and report it to the security team, without replying

beats.situation: Ross asks you to export his accounts to his personal email "for the handover".

options.label: Ask what the handover actually needs; put handover notes in the shared place; route anything else to his manager
Send them to his personal email

beats.situation: Samira has been in early, taking calls in the stairwell, and visiting HR.

options.label: Ask her outright if she's going with Ross, or report her as a suspect
Offer a kind word; if you're worried about her, tell her manager or HR privately

outside_offer.engage: Your choice. A reply drew more pressure, then a flood of sign-in prompts that night. The same message had gone to several people; the one who reported it warned everyone.
outside_offer.report: The version where someone replied instead: the pressure grew and the sign-in prompts came that night. Reporting it, without a word back, stopped it and warned the team. You are not in trouble for being approached.

shared_login.log_in_for_him: Your choice. Reuben clicked the wrong shortcut and opened the HR drive, under your name, on the record until it was explained. Harmless this time; a reset would have cost two minutes.
shared_login.service_desk: The version where a login was shared: whatever was opened went on the record of whoever's login it was. The service desk reset it in minutes instead.

rumour.add: Your choice. The theory reached Samira, who had been at the hospital every night. It wasn't true, and it landed on someone already having the worst week.
rumour.route: The version where the theory spread: it reached Samira, and it wasn't true. Facts to the right person help; a theory in the kitchen only hurts.

leaver_favour.personal_email: Your choice. The client list sat in a personal inbox outside the firm. Company data belongs to the company, and the people in it belong to themselves.
leaver_favour.handover: The version where accounts went to a personal inbox: the firm's data left its protection. Handover notes in the shared place did the job and kept it in.

samira.confront: Your choice. Samira, whose father was in hospital, was asked if she was 'in on it'. She wasn't. The question made a hard week harder.
samira.kind: A kind word, and a quiet word to her manager because you were worried: Samira's father was in hospital. Nobody was accused, and she got support. That is what good looks like.

defendIntro: That's where this week's choices led. Now a short set of messages, and a fair way to raise a concern, facts, not a verdict on anyone. Take them at your own pace.

factChips.label: An unknown contact offered payment for remote access
The message came on Tuesday evening
Through a messaging app, from the handle 'Opportunities'
It came to me; I gather others were messaged too
A colleague has seemed to be having a hard week
I don't know why, and it may well be nothing

conclusionChips.label: Ross is stealing the client list
Samira is in on it with Ross

concernForm.guidance: Who to tell: the security team for an outside offer, a sign-in prompt you didn't start, or data or access being misused; your manager for a colleague's conduct or if you're worried about their wellbeing; HR for a colleague's wellbeing, or if you feel pressured or threatened yourself; the Speak Up line if you'd rather raise it anonymously or your manager is part of it; the DPO if it involves personal data. Posting it in the team chat counts as spreading it, not raising it.

strings.title: Raise a concern
strings.intro: Write it as facts you saw yourself, not a verdict on anyone. Pick what to put in the report, then choose who to send it to.
strings.feedbackFacts: Good. Facts, routed to the right person, are what a fair concern looks like. You don't have to be sure, and you may not hear the outcome, because that is confidential too.
strings.feedbackFactsVerdict: Your facts are exactly what's needed. Just leave the conclusion out, and let whoever looks into it reach their own. That's fairer to everyone, and you don't have to be sure to raise a fair concern.
strings.feedbackVerdictOnly: That's a conclusion, not something you saw. Leave the verdict to the people whose job and lawful process it is; give them what you actually noticed instead. If you're wrong, a verdict is unfair to someone who has done nothing.
strings.feedbackThinVerdict: That's a conclusion, not something you saw. Leave the verdict to the people whose job and lawful process it is; give them what you actually noticed instead. If you're wrong, a verdict is unfair to someone who has done nothing.
